title: New Roadside Scanners Can Track Your Phone, Earbuds, and Even Your Dog
excerpt: Leonardo's SignalTrace system links Bluetooth devices to license plates, creating electronic fingerprints for vehicles. The technology arrives as Flock Safety faces a wave of police abuse scandals.
body:
• Defense contractor Leonardo is marketing SignalTrace, a system that pairs with license plate readers to track Bluetooth devices — including smartphones, earbuds, smartwatches, and even pet microchips — and links them to specific vehicles.
  • The technology creates "electronic fingerprints" by analyzing which devices repeatedly travel with a car, allowing police to identify vehicles even without license plates.
  • Flock Safety, which operates 120,000 cameras across 49 states, announced mandatory new safeguards on August 13 after a string of police abuse scandals involving officers stalking ex-partners and running unauthorized searches.
  • Privacy researchers and the ACLU warn that combining device tracking with plate readers could enable mass surveillance of associations and movements without warrants.

For years, the argument from surveillance companies was simple: license plate readers track cars, not people. That distinction is about to collapse.

A product called SignalTrace, marketed by defense contractor Leonardo, promises to turn roadside cameras into something far more powerful — a system that doesn't just photograph your license plate but also catalogues the electronic devices inside your car and links them to you over time.

How SignalTrace Works

Traditional automatic license plate readers, or ALPRs, capture an image, log a plate number, and record a timestamp and location. SignalTrace adds a parallel sensor layer. According to reporting by 404 Media, the system is designed to collect signals from Bluetooth-enabled devices — smartphones, wireless earbuds, fitness trackers, smartwatches — as well as Wi-Fi devices, RFID tags, vehicle infotainment systems, tire pressure monitoring sensors, and even pet microchips.

By analyzing which devices repeatedly travel alongside a specific vehicle, SignalTrace creates what Leonardo describes as an "electronic fingerprint" tied to that car. Over time, the system can recognize a vehicle without seeing its license plate at all — simply by identifying the cluster of devices inside it.

"Investigators may no longer need to begin with a known person or vehicle. Instead, they can begin with recurring patterns of movement and proximity, then use other records to identify the people connected to them."

— Nicole M. Bennett, Researcher, Indiana University

Leonardo's product literature states that SignalTrace "does not identify people" and "only collects electronic signatures." But privacy researchers say that framing relies on a narrow definition of identity. A recurring device signal linked to a registered vehicle, combined with location data, can effectively single out an individual — especially when cross-referenced with other records.

Flock Safety Faces Its Own Reckoning

The SignalTrace revelation arrives amid a separate crisis for the surveillance camera industry. Flock Safety, the dominant player in the ALPR market, operates 120,000 cameras across 49 states serving more than 6,000 law enforcement agencies. On August 13, the company announced mandatory new safeguards after a cascade of police abuse scandals.

A Georgia police chief was arrested in November 2025 for allegedly using Flock cameras to stalk multiple people; he was found dead by suicide before trial. In Arizona, the city of Chandler discontinued its Flock contract after detecting an "anomaly" in camera use, while an Apache Junction officer resigned after using the system to track his wife. In North Carolina, an officer was charged with unlawful computer access after allegedly searching her boyfriend's ex-wife's plate 31 times, entering fake justifications including burglary and traffic infractions.

Flock CEO Garrett Langley told USA TODAY that the company is implementing universal changes: every vehicle search will now require a specific case code tied to an active investigation, audit assistance tools that flag abnormal searches will be mandatory rather than optional, and data retention will shrink from 30 days to seven.

"A search without a reason is a search that shouldn't happen in the first place."

— Flock Safety

The Fourth Amendment Question

The legal landscape is shifting beneath these technologies. In its June 2026 decision in Chatrie v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled that obtaining anonymized location data constituted a Fourth Amendment search, even when police began with unidentified devices and worked backward to identify their owners. The ruling built on the 2018 Carpenter v. United States precedent, which established that people have a reasonable expectation of privacy in records of their physical movements.

Research underscores the risk. A study published in Scientific Reports found that just four time-and-place data points were sufficient to uniquely identify 95% of individuals in a dataset of 1.5 million people. SignalTrace, which collects device signals at fixed roadside locations over time, could generate precisely that kind of pattern.

Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union, told USA TODAY that the technology triggers concerns across the political spectrum. "There's different reasons, but everyone is arriving at the same position, which is mass government surveillance in this country has gotten completely out of control and needs to be reined in immediately," he said.

What Comes Next

SignalTrace is a tested and marketed product, not yet an established police practice. At least one installation has been identified in Oxon Hill, Maryland, and a predecessor technology appears on an official New York state contract price list. But the deeper question is whether existing legal frameworks designed for license plates can govern a system that effectively tracks the people inside the car.

For now, every Bluetooth-enabled device you carry — your phone, your earbuds, your watch — broadcasts a signal that these systems can capture. Whether that amounts to surveillance or just good policing is a question legislators, courts, and the public are only beginning to confront.
